Any species that reaches the capacity for relativistic travel should be able to extend their lifeline towards something approaching infinity, yet... apparent emptiness.

Well, right now we're stuck with the limits of Tsiolkovsky's equation (as long as we're using chemical engines), therefore any speeds where relativistic effects start to matter are our of the question. There are ideas like nuclear propulsion (see project Orion) or solar sails, but still speeds above 0.2c are hard to imagine. At 0.2c the crew would still experience 360 days to cover one LY.

Of course there are ideas like emdrive or Alcubierre drive, but one is getting less and less probable (no reviewed studies, or ideas how it could work and why it'd break the most basic laws of physics), while the other is just some trickery with equations.

...and well, even if we got something capable of accelerating to 0.99c (so the crew would experience a managable time) I doubt we'd go blindly with such missions - therefore we'd still have to send (and hear back from) robotic probes.

I never said that was an easy if! However, I do think it's an inevitable if. I am also extremely critical of the EM drive mostly because of the lack of any sound reason for why it works. However, it should be interesting to see the latest results. The latest update (from around last September) was that NASA had independently verified it generating thrust, and commissioned 3 independent labs to also build/test it independently. Assuming those tests are successful, the next test should be interesting. If we're worried about something like Earth's magnetic field somehow acting as a confounding factor then presumably even low earth orbit would be insufficient. Anyhow, something interesting to await.

I do disagree on the settlement aspect though. I think it is close to 100% certain that we will end up going on one-way settlement missions. The only issue will be money, but I imagine once we develop technologies that could even remotely possibly be developed to accommodate relativistic travel there be inconceivable amounts of money being thrown at developing and furthering it. Imagine once the billionaires learn about the potential of relativistic travel. How much are they going to be willing to pay for even a remote chance at being able patronize the medical facilities and technologies of hundreds of years in the future?

Relativity in general opens up such bizarre scenarios. Imagine we do set out on a one-way trip to a planet some 1200 light years away. And then 100 years later we make a revolutionary discovery enabling us to somehow massively increase the tolerable and viable rates of acceleration and get there in a fraction of the relativistic time. All the sudden that one way trip finally gets there after 20 years only to find not only is the planet habitable, it was colonized by humans from Earth hundreds of years ago. Reality is certainly more bizarre than any sci-fi.
